videos.title: A Washington ZIP Code Still Carries a Pre-1963 Mail Zone
videos.description:
Before ZIP codes, letters to many U.S. cities carried a short zone number, such as Washington 18, D.C. When the Zone Improvement Plan arrived on July 1, 1963, that zone number became the last two digits of Washington's ZIP Code 20018. This short history uses Library of Congress sources to trace how an old city mail zone was folded into the five-digit code.
#history #zipcode #didyouknow

videos.title: Hawaii's Rat-Fighting Mongooses Had a Scheduling Problem
videos.description:
In the 1880s, mongooses were brought into Hawaii's sugarcane fields to control rats. The plan failed because mongooses are mostly active by day and rats come out at night. According to Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, the mongooses went on to devastate native bird populations, especially ground nesters such as the threatened nēnē. Source: U.S. National Park Service, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, Invasive Animals page.
#history #hawaii #didyouknow

videos.title: Early Tin Cans Were Hand-Soldered at a Delaware Cannery
videos.description:
Early tin cans had filling holes that workers closed by hand-soldering a cap, and can-making stayed largely manual for most of the 19th century. In Dover, Delaware, the Richardson & Robbins cannery made many of its own containers, a practice it kept until 1941. The firm's records show how a food factory once built and sealed its own packaging. #CanningHistory #DidYouKnow #EverydayObjects

videos.description:

videos.title: Jefferson's Envoys Went to Buy New Orleans and Said Yes to Far More
videos.description:
President Jefferson sent James Monroe to France to join Robert Livingston, with up to ten million dollars to buy New Orleans and West Florida. As yellow fever ravaged France's army in Saint-Domingue, Napoleon dropped his Louisiana plans and offered the whole territory for fifteen million dollars. The envoys went far beyond their instructions and agreed, based on the U.S. State Department's Office of the Historian.

videos.title: A 2,500-Pound Machine of Gears Did America's Tide Math
videos.description:
Predicting a tide meant adding many smaller constituent tides into one curve, which was too much labor to do by hand. The U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey's Tide-Predicting Machine No. 2 did that adding with gears, shafts and summation chains, and a pointer on a dial showed the result. It made U.S. tide predictions from 1912 to 1965, and electronic computers took over in 1966.
#history #engineering #didyouknow

videos.title: The Teddy Bear Owes Its Name to a Refusal in Mississippi
videos.description:
In 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt refused to shoot a tied-up black bear on a Mississippi hunt because he thought it was unsportsmanlike. Cartoonist Clifford Berryman drew the moment for the Washington Post, and a Brooklyn shop owner named Morris Michtom then made a stuffed toy called Teddy's Bear. Sources: U.S. National Park Service and U.S. National Archives.
#history #teddybear #didyouknow

videos.title: U.S. Lifesavers Fired a Cannon to Rescue Shipwrecked Crews
videos.description:
When a ship ran aground near the U.S. coast, lifesavers on the beach used a small cannon to send a thin line out to the stranded ship. Army officer David Lyle designed the gun. The crew hauled heavier lines aboard, and survivors came ashore one at a time in a life ring with canvas pants sewn into it. It did not always work, and the National Park Service explains why.

videos.title: The Library of Congress Was Rebuilt From One Man's Private Bookshelves
videos.description:
In 1814, the burning of Washington destroyed the small congressional library inside the Capitol, a collection limited to law, economics and history. Congress chose to replace it with Thomas Jefferson's personal library of 6,487 volumes, which covered almost every subject. The Library of Congress still names Jefferson's idea of universality as the reason it collects so widely.
#history #libraryofcongress #thomasjefferson

videos.description: A thermostat once opened a coal furnace's damper, according to an 1886 patent by Albert Butz. videos.title: Yellowstone's Wolf Planners Expected a Third of Wolves to Add Nothing
videos.description:
In 1994, U.S. officials approved returning gray wolves to Yellowstone after a formal environmental impact statement. The planners expected about a third of released wolves to add nothing to population growth, but the 1995 founders reproduced more, died less, and roamed less than assumed, so planned Canadian transplants were judged unnecessary by 1997. #YellowstoneWolves #WildlifeHistory #EnvironmentalHistory

videos.title: Railroad Clocks Ran on Standard Time 35 Years Before U.S. Law Did
videos.description:
Before standard time, American cities set their clocks by the sun. At noon on November 18, 1883, railroad clocks across the United States were reset to a new standard time, and several cities heard noon strike twice. Congress did not pass its Standard Time Act until 1918.

videos.title: The Smithsonian Began as a Backup Plan in One Man's Will
videos.description:
James Smithson's will left most of his estate to his nephew, with a backup clause in case the nephew died without heirs. When that happened in 1835, the money went to the United States to found the Smithsonian Institution, after Congress decided whether to accept it. Smithson's reason for choosing the United States remains unknown.

videos.title: Sichuan's Ancient Water Scheme Manages a River Without Blocking It
videos.description:
Dujiangyan, in Sichuan Province, China, is an ancient irrigation system that controls the Minjiang River without a dam across it. Engineers used dikes, a floodgate and a diversion passage to split the flow and keep water reaching the Chengdu Plain's farmland. UNESCO documents the system, which still supplies farms today. #ChinaHistory #IrrigationHistory #IngeniousSolutions

videos.title: Apollo 13's Square Air Canisters Did Not Fit the Round Openings
videos.description:
On Apollo 13 in 1970, spare square carbon dioxide canisters from the command module could not connect to the lunar module's round scrubber ports. Houston teams tested a workaround in an altitude chamber, and the crew built it from a suit hose, plastic bags, a cue card and duct tape. NASA's technical brief records that carbon dioxide then fell to 1 mmHg.
#Apollo13 #SpaceHistory #NASAHistory

videos.title: Bubble Wrap Kept One Framed Photo Afloat in a New Orleans Flood
videos.description:
Weeks after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, water filled photographer Herman Leonard's New Orleans studio. Some framed prints there had been bubble-wrapped for shipping, and the wrap helped keep them from sinking, though water still damaged the edges. This is one documented studio case, not proof of how bubble wrap performs in floods generally.

videos.title: The Panama Canal Builders Bought Wire Screens Against Mosquitoes
videos.description:
In the early 1900s, the US canal project in Panama faced yellow fever and malaria among its workers. Investigators had linked the fever to mosquitoes breeding in standing water, and the Isthmian Canal Commission chose to pay for wire screens rather than save the money. Sources credit the sanitation program led by William Gorgas as a major factor in completing the canal, though not its only cause. #PanamaCanal #WorldHistory #Sanitation

After the 1913 flood and abandonment, the old canal corridor became the spine of a national park, and its towpath now serves hikers and cyclists. Sources also note the canals had already fallen into disuse, so the flood was not the only cause.

videos.title: Why Did Ajanta's Buddhists Carve Their Caves Twice, Centuries Apart?
videos.description: The Ajanta Caves in Maharashtra, India, were cut into a cliff in two separate phases about four centuries apart. The change in how Buddhists worshipped the Buddha helps explain why the second wave looks so different. UNESCO describes their paintings and sculptures as masterpieces of Buddhist art. #Ajanta #IndianHistory #WorldHeritage

videos.title: Were These Manila Police Really Former Rebels?
videos.description:
A 1901 stereograph from the Library of Congress shows Filipino police in Manila, with a caption calling them former insurgents. The photo's own title is the only source for that claim, so the story behind it is about what the caption says and what can be verified. Part of The Story Behind This Photo series. #PhilippineHistory #PhotoHistory #HiddenHistory

videos.title: Who First Turned a Cactus Insect Into the World's Reddest Red?
videos.description:
Cochineal is a red dye made from a scale insect that lives on cactus plants in Latin America. Indigenous peoples of the Americas used it long before European contact, and it once ranked among the world's most important dyes. Its reds still appear in cosmetics, textiles and medicines today.

videos.title: What Were Apollo 12 Astronauts Doing at an Old Moon Probe?
videos.description: On 19 November 1969, Apollo 12 landed on the Moon close to Surveyor 3, a robotic probe that had been sitting there since 1967. The crew photographed the probe and removed parts from it, a visit that showed how precisely a lunar landing could be made. #SpaceHistory #Apollo12 #WorldHistory

videos.title: How Close Did a Million Artworks Come to Staying Behind?
videos.description:
In 1941, the Hermitage Museum in Leningrad packed its collections for evacuation as the Second World War reached the Soviet Union. The museum's own history describes how a third train was never able to leave before the city was cut off. Here is how the collections were saved and returned.
#HermitageMuseum #WorldWarII #RussianHistory

videos.title: Why Did China's Ming Government Abandon Its Paper Money?
videos.description: A 1375 Ming dynasty paper banknote survives in London's British Museum, showing China issued paper money centuries before most of Europe. We look at why the state wanted paper, and why people eventually turned back to silver. #ChinaHistory #MingDynasty #WorldHistory

videos.title: Was Japan Really Locked Shut for 200 Years?
videos.description:
Many students learn that Japan closed its doors completely for about two centuries. The Library of Congress describes the sakoku period as relative seclusion, with limited contact at Nagasaki and rules over trade and relations. This short video explains what the policy actually did and how it ended.
